I ran one job on IQM's free Emerald test device (emerald:mock). The job ID is 01a16483-859f-75dd-b8bd-62c86773e8b6. It holds 4 circuits with 250 shots each, and it completed. The test device is free, so it used no credits.

What I built: each circuit uses all 54 qubits as a 54-atom sheet. I read the coupler list from the real Emerald today. Real Emerald lists 85 CZ couplers. The test device lists 90, so I used only the 85 that real Emerald lists. Every qubit starts in 0. One step turns every qubit by RX(theta). Then every one of the 85 couplers gets one RZZ(-pi/2) gate. I ran 3 steps and then measured all 54 qubits.

I sent the circuits in the chip's own native gates, so no compiler step ran. Each coupler gate became exactly one CZ. The extra Z turns that RZZ needs were folded into the phases of the next RX pulses. I checked this rewrite against the plain RX and RZZ circuit on a small test graph, and the two gave the same probabilities. I read the circuits back from the server. Each circuit has 255 CZ gates (85 couplers times 3 steps) and measures QB1 through QB54.

Magnetization is the average of Z over all 54 qubits. Z is +1 for bit 0 and -1 for bit 1.
- theta = 0: ideal 1.000. The test device gave -0.010.
- theta = 0.2 pi: ideal 0.452. The test device gave -0.016.
- theta = 0.35 pi: ideal 0.113. The test device gave -0.007.
- theta = 0.5 pi: ideal 0.000. The test device gave +0.017.

What a perfect quantum computer would show: with no sideways field (theta = 0), every spin stays up and the magnetization is 1. As the field gets stronger, it tips the spins over. The neighbor couplings then spread and scramble that tipping across the sheet. The magnetization falls to 0.45, then to 0.11, and reaches 0 at theta = 0.5 pi. A stronger sideways field melts the sheet's magnetization faster.

To get the ideal numbers I did not simulate all 54 qubits at once. The value for one qubit after 3 steps depends only on qubits within 2 couplers of it. That group is at most 13 qubits, so I simulated it exactly. I checked this shortcut against a full simulation of a 15-qubit grid, and the two matched.

Why the measured numbers do not follow the curve: the test device does not simulate the circuit. It checks that the job is valid and returns made-up bits. All four circuits came back near 0 magnetization, even the theta = 0 circuit, which should give 1. These measured numbers do not show any physics. To see the real melting curve, the same job would have to run on the real Emerald, and that costs credits.

The counts bitstrings list the qubits in order QB1 to QB54, from left to right. The "counts" field holds the last circuit (theta = 0.5 pi). Scripts and results are in /Users/claytonchancey/Desktop/quantum/.claude/worktrees/wf_8d7e6233-d69-4 (kicked.py, submit.py, result.json, job_log.txt).
